claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the functional data presented in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The structure of SLC26A6 was determined by cryo-electron microscopy at 3.3 Å resolution.
claims.source: A dataset of the protein purified in the detergent glycol-diosgenin (GDN) at 3.3 Å was of high quality and allowed for the unambiguous interpretation of the cryo-EM density by an atomic model (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2,Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claims.claim: The SLC26A6 structure shows familiar features that have previously been observed in various eukaryotic family members including human and murine SLC26A9, SLC26A5, SLC26A4, and the plant transporter AtSULTR4.
claims.source: In its organization, the SLC26A6 structure shows familiar features that have previously been observed in various eukaryotic family members of known structure including human and murine SLC26A9 (Chi et al., 2020; Walter et al., 2019), SLC26A5 (Bavi et al., 2021; Butan et al., 2022; Futamata et al., 2022; Ge et al., 2021), SLC26A4 (Liu et al., 2023) and the plant transporter AtSULTR4 (Wang et al., 2021; Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison with prior structures cited in the text.

claims.claim: The SLC26A6 subunit consists of a membrane-inserted unit (TM) followed by a cytoplasmic STAS domain.
claims.source: The SLC26A6 subunit consists of a membrane-inserted unit (TM) followed by a cytoplasmic STAS domain.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: In the homodimeric SLC26A6 protein, subunit interactions are predominantly formed by the domain-swapped cytoplasmic parts including an extended N-terminal region and the C-terminal STAS domain.
claims.source: In the homodimeric protein, subunit interactions are predominantly formed by the domain-swapped cytoplasmic parts including an extended N-terminal region and the C-terminal STAS domain, whereas the few contacts between the transmembrane transport units are confined to the end of the terminal membrane-spanning helix α14 (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: A region connecting secondary structure elements of the STAS domain (located between Cα1 and β4) termed the intervening sequence (IVS) is present in SLC26A6.
claims.source: A region connecting secondary structure elements of the STAS domain (located between Cα1 and β4) termed the intervening sequence (IVS) is present in the characterized protein (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Removal of the IVS region increased both the stability and surface expression of a construct of the murine SLC26A9 while retaining its transport properties.
claims.source: Previously, removal of this region increased both the stability and surface expression of a construct of the murine SLC26A9 while retaining its transport properties (Walter et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: In the SLC26A6 structure, the N-terminal part of the IVS folds into an α-helix encompassing amino acids 569–593 (CαIVS) whereas the following 61 residues are unstructured and thus not resolved in the density.
claims.source: In the density, the N-terminal part of the IVS folds into an α-helix encompassing amino acids 569–593 (CαIVS) whereas the following 61 residues are unstructured and thus not resolved in the density (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: On the C-terminus of the IVS, the density re-appears at Ser 655 at the region preceding β4, which interacts with CαIVS.
claims.source: On the C-terminus of the IVS, the density re-appears at Ser 655 at the region preceding β4, which interacts with CαIVS (Figure 2B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claims.claim: A generally similar arrangement of the IVS was also observed in a full-length construct of human SLC26A9.
claims.source: A generally similar arrangement was also observed in a full-length construct of human SLC26A9 (Chi et al., 2020; Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and comparison shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: In both SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 structures, CαIVS runs about parallel to the membrane plane and contacts the loop connecting α8 and α9 of the mobile core domain.
claims.source: In both structures, CαIVS runs about parallel to the membrane plane and contacts the loop connecting α8 and α9 of the mobile core domain.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claims.claim: The interaction between CαIVS and the core domain loop presumably influences the conformational preferences of the core domain thereby potentially impacting transport.
claims.source: This presumably influences its conformational preferences thereby potentially impacting transport (Figure 2B–D).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural observation.

claims.claim: In the dimeric SLC26A6 transporter, the two TMs share minimal contacts and thus supposedly function as independent units.
claims.source: In the dimeric transporter, the two TMs share minimal contacts and thus supposedly function as independent units (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Structural differences underlying the distinct transport properties of SLC26 paralogs are expected to be manifested in the TM part of the protein.
claims.source: Consequently, we expect structural differences underlying the distinct transport properties of SLC26 paralogs to be manifested in this part of the protein.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural organization.

claims.claim: The TMs of SLC26A6 consist of two topologically related repeats of seven transmembrane segments, which span the membrane with opposite orientation.
claims.source: Like in other pro- and eukaryotic family members of known structure, the TMs of SLC26A6 consist of two topologically related repeats of seven transmembrane segments, which span the membrane with opposite orientation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: Elements of both repeats in the TM are intertwined to form two segregated modules, a gate domain and a core domain.
claims.source: Elements of both repeats are intertwined to form two segregated modules, a gate domain and a core domain (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The TMs of SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 superimpose with an RMSD of 1.3 Å, illustrating their equivalence.
claims.source: The equivalence between the SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 conformations is illustrated in the overlay of the respective TMs whose Cα positions superimpose with an RMSD of 1.3 Å (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Both SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 conformations represent inward-facing states of transporters presumably functioning by an alternate access mechanism.
claims.source: Both conformations represent inward-facing states of transporters presumably functioning by an alternate access mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and knowledge of transporter mechanisms.

claims.claim: The substrate binding site located in the center of the core domain is accessible from the cytoplasm via a spacious aqueous cavity, whereas the extracellular exit is sealed by extended contacts between core and gate domains.
claims.source: The substrate binding site located in the center of the core domain is accessible from the cytoplasm via a spacious aqueous cavity, whereas the extracellular exit is sealed by extended contacts between core and gate domains (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3C, D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claims.claim: The resemblance between individual sub-domains of SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 exceeds the overall similarity of the TM, with core- and gate domains superimposing with RMSDs of 1.13 Å and 1.2 Å, respectively.
claims.source: The resemblance between individual sub-domains even exceeds the overall similarity of the TM (with core- and gate domains superimposing with RMSDs of 1.13 Å and 1.2 Å, respectively) distinguishing them as largely independent units of a modular protein (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The gate domains of SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 do not show pronounced differences.
claims.source: In the comparison of both paralogs, the gate domains do not show pronounced differences (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The gate domains together with the cytoplasmic STAS domains form a contiguous rigid scaffold of the dimeric protein that presumably remains static during transport.
claims.source: Together with the cytoplasmic STAS domains, which constitute the bulk of the dimer interface, these sub-domains form a contiguous rigid scaffold of the dimeric protein that presumably remains static during transport (Figure 2B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Both core domains represent the mobile elements of the protein.
claims.source: In contrast, both core domains represent the mobile elements of the protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and knowledge of transporter mechanisms.

claims.claim: Each core domain carries a substrate binding site located in a pocket at the center of the unit facing the gate domain.
claims.source: Each core domain carries a substrate binding site located in a pocket at the center of the unit facing the gate domain (Figures 3C, D ,, 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figures 3C, D and 4A.

claims.claim: The presumable location of a bound chloride ion is resolved in the structure of SLC26A6 at a low contour of the map.
claims.source: The presumable location of a bound chloride ion is resolved in the structure of SLC26A6 at a low contour of the map (Figure 4B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: The position of the bound chloride in SLC26A6 concurs with positions inferred from known structures of paralogs, which show binding of Cl- and HCO3- to an equivalent location.
claims.source: This position concurs with positions inferred from known structures of paralogs, which show binding of Cl- and HCO3- to an equivalent location (Chi et al., 2020; Futamata et al., 2022; Ge et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023; Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison with prior structures cited in the text.

claims.claim: The anion binding site is placed between the opposed short helices α3 and α10, which partly span the membrane and whose N-termini are aligned to face each other in the center of the core domain.
claims.source: The anion binding site is placed between the opposed short helices α3 and α10, which partly span the membrane and whose N-termini are aligned to face each other in the center of the core domain (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Together with the side chains of surrounding residues, both α-helix termini form a selective anion binding site.
claims.source: Together with the side chains of surrounding residues, both α-helix termini form a selective anion binding site (Figure 4B–G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4B–G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In complex with its bound cargo, the core domain is believed to shuttle as rigid unit between two extreme conformations where the binding site is either exposed to the cytoplasm or the extracellular environment.
claims.source: In complex with its bound cargo, the core domain is believed to shuttle as rigid unit between two extreme conformations where the binding site is either exposed to the cytoplasm or the extracellular environment (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and knowledge of elevator-type transport mechanisms.

claims.claim: The core domains presumably display the characteristic features accounting for the distinct functional properties of SLC26A6 and SLC26A9.
claims.source: As carrier of the substrate binding site, the core domains presumably display the characteristic features accounting for the distinct functional properties of SLC26A6 and SLC26A9.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and functional differences.

claims.claim: The conservation of core domains within the SLC26 family is illustrated in the comparison of the respective domains of SLC26A6 and SLC26A5 (Prestin).
claims.source: Their conservation within the SLC26 family is illustrated in the comparison of the respective domains of SLC26A6 and SLC26A5 (Prestin; Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, C, D, E, G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: SLC26A5 belongs to a protein that confers electromotility instead of transporting ions.
claims.source: Latter belongs to a protein that, instead of transporting ions, confers electromotility and which in the best defined structure (PDBID: 7LGU) resides in a distinct conformation where the substrate binding site has become buried between core and gate domain (leading to an RMSD of 2.9 Å for the entire TMD; Ge et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Despite the functional and conformational differences, the core domains of SLC26A5 and SLC26A6 superimpose with an RMSD of only 1.13 Å, illustrating their close structural resemblance.
claims.source: Despite the functional and conformational differences, the core domains of SLC26A5 and SLC26A6 superimpose with an RMSD of only 1.13 Å, illustrating their close structural resemblance (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, C.

claims.claim: SLC26A6 and SLC26A5 share similar ion binding properties that extend to Cl- and HCO3-, latter of which is not a substrate of SLC26A9.
claims.source: Both proteins share similar ion binding properties that extends to Cl- and HCO3-, latter of which is not a substrate of SLC26A9 (Walter et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and the current structural data.

claims.claim: The comparison of the core domains of SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 shows distinct features that likely underlie the differences in substrate selectivity and transport mechanism.
claims.source: In contrast to the general similarity with SLC26A5, the comparison of the same units of SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 shows distinct features that likely underlie the differences in substrate selectivity and transport mechanism (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C.

claims.claim: The differences between SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 core domains are confined to the conformation of α10, which at its N-terminus forms direct interactions with transported ions, whereas the remainder of the domain is very similar.
claims.source: These are confined to the conformation of α10, which at its N-terminus forms direct interactions with transported ions, whereas the remainder of the domain is very similar (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C.

claims.claim: The difference in the conformations of α10 between SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 can be approximated by a 12–14° rotation of α10 of SLC26A9 around an axis located at its C-terminal end towards α-helix 1.
claims.source: The difference in the conformations of this short membrane-inserted helix can be approximated by a 12–14° rotation of α10 of SLC26A9 around an axis located at its C-terminal end towards α-helix 1 (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C.

claims.claim: The replacement of residues within the contact region of SLC26A9 in comparison to other family members acts to lower their side chain volume at the contact region between α1 and α10.
claims.source: The replacement of residues within the contact region of SLC26A9 in comparison to other family members acts to lower their side chain volume at the contact region between both helices (Figure 4C–F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4C–F.

claims.claim: Ser 96 and Val 100 on SLC26A6 are both replaced by glycines at equivalent positions in SLC26A9 (i.e., Gly 77 and Gly 81).
claims.source: These include Ser 96 and Val 100 on SLC26A6, which are both replaced by glycines at equivalent positions in SLC26A9 (i.e., Gly 77 and Gly 81) and a substitution of Val 407, Gln 408 and Thr 411 by Ala 396, Val 397 and Ala 400 (Figure 4C–F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4C–F.

claims.claim: Val 407, Gln 408 and Thr 411 in SLC26A6 are substituted by Ala 396, Val 397 and Ala 400 in SLC26A9.
claims.source: These include Ser 96 and Val 100 on SLC26A6, which are both replaced by glycines at equivalent positions in SLC26A9 (i.e., Gly 77 and Gly 81) and a substitution of Val 407, Gln 408 and Thr 411 by Ala 396, Val 397 and Ala 400 (Figure 4C–F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4C–F.

claims.claim: There are differences in the side chains surrounding the ion binding site between SLC26A6 and SLC26A9, which together determine the size and polarity of the substrate binding pocket.
claims.source: In addition to the described substitutions, there are also differences in the side chains surrounding the ion binding site, which together determine the size and polarity of the substrate binding pocket (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Ser 401 of SLC26A6 is replaced by an alanine in SLC26A9 (Ala 390).
claims.source: These differences extend to Ser 401 of SLC26A6, which is replaced by an alanine in SLC26A9 (Ala 390), and most prominent, the large Arg 404 of SLC26A6, which is replaced by Val 393 in SLC26A9 (Figure 4C-I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4C-I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–G.

claims.claim: The large Arg 404 of SLC26A6 is replaced by Val 393 in SLC26A9.
claims.source: These differences extend to Ser 401 of SLC26A6, which is replaced by an alanine in SLC26A9 (Ala 390), and most prominent, the large Arg 404 of SLC26A6, which is replaced by Val 393 in SLC26A9 (Figure 4C-I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4C-I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–G.

claims.claim: The pocket is considerably deeper in SLC26A9 compared to SLC26A6, where it is delimited by the side chain of Arg 404 that interacts with the residues preceding α helix 3 to form the back side of the shallow binding site.
claims.source: As a result, the pocket is considerably deeper in SLC26A9 compared SLC26A6, where it is delimited by the side chain of Arg 404 that interacts with the residues preceding α helix 3 to form the back side of the shallow binding site (Figure 4D–I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4D–I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–H.

claims.claim: Arg 404 likely contributes to the stabilization of bound anions by coulombic interactions, with its guanidium group potentially engaging in direct interactions with bicarbonate or oxalate.
claims.source: In addition to its structural role, Arg 404 likely also contributes to the stabilization of bound anions by coulombic interactions, with its guanidium group potentially engaging in direct interactions with bicarbonate or oxalate.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural observation and chemical properties of arginine.

claims.claim: The altered geometry of the binding site leads to the binding of Cl- deeper in the pocket in case of SLC26A9.
claims.source: The altered geometry of the site leads to the binding of Cl- deeper in the pocket in case of SLC26A9 (Figure 4D, E,G-I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H) and presumably explains why bicarbonate interacts with SLC26A6 but not SLC26A9.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4D, E, G-I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claims.claim: The altered geometry of the binding site presumably explains why bicarbonate interacts with SLC26A6 but not SLC26A9.
claims.source: The altered geometry of the site leads to the binding of Cl- deeper in the pocket in case of SLC26A9 (Figure 4D, E,G-I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H) and presumably explains why bicarbonate interacts with SLC26A6 but not SLC26A9.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural differences.

claims.claim: The mutation R404V in SLC26A6 is well-tolerated and does not interfere with protein integrity as judged by its expression level and biochemical properties.
claims.source: This mutation is well-tolerated and does not interfere with protein integrity as judged by its expression level and biochemical properties.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the functional data presented in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Small currents were detected for SLC26A6 R404V in whole-cell patch clamp experiments in symmetric Cl- solutions, which are low compared to SLC26A9.
claims.source: In whole-cell patch clamp experiments, we detected small currents in symmetric Cl- solutions, which are low compared to SLC26A9, despite the comparable expression of the mutant at the cell-surface (Figure 5B–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B–E.

claims.claim: The currents detected for SLC26A6 R404V are not significantly higher than SLC26A6 WT.
claims.source: Irrespective of their magnitude, which is not significantly higher than SLC26A6 WT (Figure 5C and D), these currents are indicative for the capability of the mutant to mediate electrogenic Cl- transport at low rates.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claims.claim: The currents detected for SLC26A6 R404V are indicative for the capability of the mutant to mediate electrogenic Cl- transport at low rates.
claims.source: Irrespective of their magnitude, which is not significantly higher than SLC26A6 WT (Figure 5C and D), these currents are indicative for the capability of the mutant to mediate electrogenic Cl- transport at low rates.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiology data.

claims.claim: The proteoliposome-based ACMA assay confirmed that the R404V mutation has conferred the ability to SLC26A6 to pass downhill Cl- transport.
claims.source: We thus turned to our proteoliposome-based ACMA assay to confirm that side chain replacement has indeed conferred the ability to SLC26A6 to pass downhill Cl- transport (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: The mutant SLC26A6 R404V did not show pronounced Cl- flux in the lucigenin assay for coupled Cl-/HCO3- exchange.
claims.source: After demonstrating uncoupled chloride transport, we tested whether the mutant has retained its ability of mediating coupled Cl-/HCO3- exchange using the fluorophore lucigenin but did not find pronounced Cl- flux in this case (Figure 5G and H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5G and H.

claims.claim: The mutation of a conserved basic position in the ion binding site has compromised the ability of SLC26A6 to mediate coupled Cl-/HCO3- exchange and instead facilitated uncoupled Cl- transport with slow kinetics.
claims.source: Together our data suggest that the mutation of a conserved basic position in the ion binding site has compromised the ability of SLC26A6 to mediate coupled Cl-/HCO3- exchange and instead facilitated uncoupled Cl- transport with slow kinetics.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the functional data presented in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The mutation of a single residue is insufficient to confer the complete functional phenotype of SLC26A9 as a fast uncoupled Cl- conductor.
claims.source: While these findings underline the importance of Arg 404 for anion interactions and coupling, they also emphasize that the mutation of a single residue is insufficient to confer the complete functional phenotype of SLC26A9 as a fast uncoupled Cl- conductor.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data of the R404V mutant.

claims.claim: The results underline the importance of the anion binding site in SLC26 transporters for the transport mechanism of its members.
claims.source: Nevertheless, our results further underline the importance of the anion binding site in SLC26 transporters for the transport mechanism of its members.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural and functional data.

claims.claim: SLC26A6 mediates electroneutral Cl-/HCO3- exchange.
claims.source: The protein mediates electroneutral Cl-/ HCO3- and presumable electrogenic Cl-/oxalate exchange, which is in stark contrast to the uncoupled Cl- transport of SLC26A9.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the functional data presented in Figure 1.

claims.claim: SLC26A6 mediates presumable electrogenic Cl-/oxalate exchange.
claims.source: The protein mediates electroneutral Cl-/ HCO3- and presumable electrogenic Cl-/oxalate exchange, which is in stark contrast to the uncoupled Cl- transport of SLC26A9.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the functional data presented in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: The altered ion binding site in SLC26A6 is located in the mobile core domain of the transmembrane transport unit.
claims.source: This is accomplished by an altered ion binding site located in the mobile core domain of the transmembrane transport unit.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claims.claim: In the case of Cl-/HCO3- transport by SLC26A6, there is a strict equimolar exchange of anions binding to a conserved site in the mobile core domain of the transmembrane transport unit.
claims.source: In the case of Cl-/HCO3- transport, we detect a strict equimolar exchange of anions binding to a conserved site in the mobile core domain of the transmembrane transport unit (Figure 4B and H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the functional and structural data presented in Figures 1 and 4.

claims.claim: An analogous mechanism is assumed for Cl-/oxalate exchange by SLC26A6.
claims.source: Although not shown unambiguously, we assume an analogous mechanism also for Cl-/oxalate exchange.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the functional data.

claims.claim: Transport by SLC26A6 would be electroneutral in case of the monovalent HCO3- and electrogenic in case of the divalent oxalate.
claims.source: Consequently, transport would be electroneutral in case of the monovalent HCO3- and electrogenic in case of the divalent oxalate (Figure 1E–H), which was already proposed in a previous study (Chernova et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the functional data and citation to prior work.

claims.claim: SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 show different features with respect to substrate selectivity and coupling.
claims.source: Regarding their function, SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 show different features with respect to substrate selectivity and coupling (Ohana et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the functional data and citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Both SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 are capable of interacting with Cl- with similar mM affinity.
claims.source: Remarkably, both proteins are capable of interacting with Cl- with similar mM affinity (Figure 1F; Walter et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the functional data shown in Figure 1F and citation to prior work.

claims.claim: SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 interact with Cl- via distinct interactions in equivalent binding regions.
claims.source: However, they do this via distinct interactions in equivalent binding regions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in Figure 4.

claims.claim: In SLC26A9, Cl- binds in a deep pocket with low field strength.
claims.source: In SLC26A9, Cl- binds in a deep pocket with low field strength, whereas the same pocket is shallower in SLC26A6, where a conserved arginine (Arg 404) increases the positive electrostatic potential and thus likely stabilizes the bound anion (Figure 4H, I and Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4H, I and Figure 6.

claims.claim: In SLC26A6, the Cl- binding pocket is shallower, where a conserved arginine (Arg 404) increases the positive electrostatic potential and thus likely stabilizes the bound anion.
claims.source: In SLC26A9, Cl- binds in a deep pocket with low field strength, whereas the same pocket is shallower in SLC26A6, where a conserved arginine (Arg 404) increases the positive electrostatic potential and thus likely stabilizes the bound anion (Figure 4H, I and Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4H, I and Figure 6.

claims.claim: Together with the presence of additional residues at the binding site (i.e., Ser 401 at the N-terminal end of α10), the captured Cl- in SLC26A6 can rely on a larger density of polar interactions.
claims.source: Together with the presence of additional residues at the binding site (i.e., Ser 401 at the N-terminal end of α10), the captured Cl- in SLC26A6 thus can rely on a larger density of polar interactions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, F.

claims.claim: The binding site in SLC26A6 likely provides a suitable environment for HCO3- and oxalate, neither of which are substrates of SLC26A9.
claims.source: The same site likely also provides a suitable environment for HCO3- and oxalate, neither of which are substrates of SLC26A9 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,H; Dorwart et al., 2007; Walter et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and functional properties.

claims.claim: A similar anion interaction observed in SLC26A6 is also found in the paralogs SLC26A4 (Pendrin) and SLC26A5 (Prestin), which both share a similar substrate preference.
claims.source: A similar anion interaction observed in SLC26A6 is also found in the paralogs SLC26A4 (Pendrin) (Liu et al., 2023) and SLC26A5 (Prestin) (Futamata et al., 2022; Ge et al., 2021), which both share a similar substrate preference.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claims.claim: The similarity between the core domains of SLC26A6 and Prestin is remarkable in light of the altered function of Prestin, which is no longer capable of transporting ions and instead operates as motor protein in cochlear outer hair cells of mammals.
claims.source: The similarity between the core domains of SLC26A6 and Prestin is remarkable in light of the altered function of the latter, which is no longer capable of transporting ions and instead operates as motor protein in cochlear outer hair cells of mammals (Zheng et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Prestin undergoes comparable conformational changes as other family members to some degree, as illustrated in the close relationship between occluded conformations of SLC26A9 and SLC26A5.

results.result: The cryo-EM structure of human SLC26A6 was determined at 3.3 Å resolution, revealing an inward-facing conformation that closely resembles SLC26A9. The structure shows a homodimeric architecture with membrane-inserted transport domains (TM) and cytoplasmic STAS domains, where the TM segregates into mobile core and static gate domains.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C57-C83 collectively describe the structural determination and characterization of SLC26A6. The cryo-EM data at 3.3 Å resolution (C57, Figure 2, Table 1) provides high-quality structural information. The structural comparisons with SLC26A9 showing RMSD values of 1.3 Å for TMs and 1.13 Å for core domains (C72, C75) are well-documented in Figures 2-3. The identification of core and gate domains, substrate binding site, and bound chloride ion are supported by the density maps and structural analysis (Figures 3-4).

results.result: SLC26A6 functions as an electroneutral Cl-/HCO3- exchanger with a Km of 16-37 mM for chloride. Unlike SLC26A9, no electrogenic currents were detected by patch clamp, but transport was demonstrated using lucigenin and europium probe assays in proteoliposomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C50 establish SLC26A6 as an electroneutral coupled exchanger through multiple complementary assays. The absence of currents in patch clamp (C40, Figure 1B) combined with surface expression confirmation (C41, Figure 1C), lucigenin-based Cl- flux measurements (C44, Figure 1E), and HCO3- transport using the europium probe (C48-C49, Figure 1G) provide converging evidence. The Km determination (C46, Figure 1F) and lack of valinomycin requirement (C45) support electroneutral exchange.

results.result: SLC26A6 mediates electrogenic Cl-/oxalate exchange, as demonstrated by ACMA fluorescence assays showing concentration-dependent oxalate transport. The 1:1 stoichiometry with divalent oxalate results in electrogenic transport, though this could not be detected by patch clamp likely due to slow kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C55, C113, C116-C117 describe oxalate transport by SLC26A6. The ACMA assay data (C54, Figure 1H) shows robust, concentration-dependent oxalate transport. The inference of electrogenic transport based on charge imbalance (C53, C117) is logically sound given the divalent nature of oxalate. The failure to detect currents by patch clamp (C55) is reasonably attributed to slow kinetics, consistent with the ACMA time course data.

results.result: The altered anion selectivity between SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 results from a remodeled ion binding site in the core domain. Key differences include a 12-14° rotation of helix α10, amino acid substitutions (particularly Arg404 in SLC26A6 vs Val393 in SLC26A9), and altered binding pocket geometry that creates a shallower, higher field-strength pocket in SLC26A6 suitable for HCO3- and oxalate binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C90-C102, C114, C120-C124 describe structural basis for selectivity differences. The structural comparisons are well-documented with RMSD calculations, specific residue identifications, and pocket geometry analysis (Figures 4C-I). The identification of Arg404 as a key residue is supported by sequence alignments (C98, Figure 4C) and structural data showing its role in delimiting the binding pocket (C99, Figure 4D-I). The inference that pocket geometry explains HCO3- selectivity (C102) is reasonable given the structural and functional data.

results.result: The R404V mutation in SLC26A6 compromises coupled Cl-/HCO3- exchange and confers slow uncoupled Cl- transport, as shown by small electrogenic currents and ACMA assay results. However, the mutation does not fully recapitulate the fast transport kinetics of SLC26A9, indicating that additional structural features are required.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C111 describe the functional consequences of the R404V mutation. The data show the mutant is well-expressed (C103, Figure 5E), exhibits small currents not significantly different from WT (C104-C105, Figure 5B-D), demonstrates uncoupled transport in ACMA assay (C107, Figure 5F), and loses coupled exchange activity (C108, Figure 5G-H). The conclusion that a single mutation is insufficient to fully convert function (C110) is supported by the slow kinetics observed compared to SLC26A9. This represents a well-designed structure-function experiment.

results.result: SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 are mechanistically distinguished by their transport cycles: SLC26A6 mediates strict 1:1 electroneutral Cl-/HCO3- exchange where unloaded state transitions are kinetically unfavorable, while SLC26A9 rapidly transitions between inward- and outward-facing states in unloaded conformations, enabling fast uncoupled transport.
results.evaluation: Claims C112, C115, C118-C119, C129-C131 synthesize the mechanistic differences between the two paralogs. The electroneutral exchange by SLC26A6 (C112, C115) is supported by the functional data in Figure 1. The similar Cl- affinities (C119) but different kinetic behaviors are well-documented. The mechanistic model (C129-C131, Figure 6) integrating structural and functional data provides a coherent explanation for the observed differences, though the exact energy barriers remain to be fully elucidated.

results.result: The core domains of SLC26A6 show high structural conservation with SLC26A5 (Prestin) despite functional differences, with an RMSD of 1.13 Å. Both share similar ion binding properties for Cl- and HCO3-, and the conserved arginine residue at the binding site is found across multiple family members including SLC26A4 and SLC26A5.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C89, C125-C128 describe structural conservation within the SLC26 family. The RMSD comparison with Prestin (C88, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) demonstrates close structural similarity despite Prestin's altered function as a motor protein (C87, C126). The shared ion binding properties (C89) and conserved arginine residue across paralogs (C125) are supported by structural comparisons and citations to prior work. This contextualizes SLC26A6 within the broader family.

results.result: The intervening sequence (IVS) region of the STAS domain contacts the core domain and may influence conformational preferences and transport activity. Removal of the IVS in SLC26A9 previously increased stability and activity, and similar interactions are observed in SLC26A6, though the functional significance in cellular environments remains unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C62, C67, C137-C143 discuss the IVS region and its potential regulatory role. While the structural observations of IVS-core domain contacts are documented (C137, Figure 2C), the functional implications are largely speculative (C67, C139, C143). The citation to prior work on IVS removal effects (C62, C138) provides some support, but the mechanistic understanding is incomplete. The role of C-terminal extensions (C141-C143) is acknowledged as unclear, indicating this area requires further investigation.

results.result: The molecular basis for the kinetic differences between coupled and uncoupled SLC26 transporters remains unclear. While conformational changes likely involve interactions between mobile core and static gate domains, the nature of the energy barrier preventing unloaded state transitions in coupled exchangers has not been elucidated, and a leaky channel-like conformation in SLC26A9 cannot be excluded.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C136 acknowledge limitations in mechanistic understanding. These claims appropriately identify knowledge gaps (C132, C134) and present reasonable hypotheses about domain interactions (C135) while noting the lack of pronounced differences in core-gate contacts between paralogs (C136, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The acknowledgment of alternative mechanisms like a channel-like conformation (C133) demonstrates scientific rigor. This honest assessment of uncertainties is appropriate for a discussion section.

results.result: Murine SLC26A9 mediates large, selective chloride currents that reverse at the Nernst potential, lack time-dependence, and show a lyotropic permeability sequence (Cl-, isothiocyanate, I-, nitrate) while discriminating against sulfate and HCO3-, characterizing it as an uncoupled chloride transporter with channel-like properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C38, C26-C27 describe SLC26A9 functional properties based on prior work and current data (Figure 1A). These claims are well-supported by citations to Walter et al., 2019 and Dorwart et al., 2007, and serve as important controls for comparison with SLC26A6. The characterization is consistent with established literature and provides the functional context for understanding mechanistic differences.

results.result: The introduction establishes the SLC26 family as conserved anion transporters with diverse mechanisms (uncoupled, coupled, motor proteins) across kingdoms of life. In humans, 10 functional paralogs show mechanistic breadth, with most operating as coupled exchangers while SLC26A9 functions as an uncoupled Cl- transporter. The structural basis for mechanistic distinctions between paralogs like SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 remained elusive prior to this study.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C34 provide background context supported by extensive citations to prior literature. These claims establish the scientific rationale for the study by describing the SLC26 family diversity (C1, C11-C18), the specific properties of SLC26A6 (C29-C33) and SLC26A9 (C18-C27), and the knowledge gap being addressed (C34). The background is well-documented with appropriate citations and accurately represents the state of the field.

results.result: Prior structural work on murine SLC26A9 established the homodimeric architecture and elevator-type transport mechanism that serves as a reference for understanding SLC26A6. The core domain shuttles as a rigid unit between inward- and outward-facing conformations, and structural differences in the TM are expected to underlie functional distinctions between paralogs.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C6, C68-C69, C84-C85 reference prior structural work on SLC26A9 that provides the framework for interpreting SLC26A6 structure. These claims are supported by citations to Walter et al., 2019 and serve to contextualize the current findings. The inferences about domain mobility and functional implications (C84-C85) are reasonable based on the structural data and established transporter mechanisms.

results.result: The study provides novel insight into the structural basis of substrate selectivity and mechanistic distinction between uncoupled and coupled SLC26 transporters, establishing a foundation for future investigations.
results.evaluation: Claim C144 is a summary statement that accurately reflects the contributions of the study. The work has indeed provided new structural information on SLC26A6, characterized its function as a coupled exchanger, identified key structural determinants of selectivity (particularly Arg404), and demonstrated functional consequences through mutagenesis. This represents a significant advance in understanding SLC26 family mechanisms.

results.result: The authors determined the cryo-EM structure of full-length human SLC26A6 at 3.3 Å resolution, revealing a homodimeric architecture with membrane-inserted transport domains (TM) and cytoplasmic STAS domains. The structure includes the first partial view of the intervening sequence (IVS) region of the STAS domain, with the N-terminal part forming an α-helix (Cα^IVS) that contacts the mobile core domain.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly praised the structural work. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'present a novel cryo-EM structure of full-length human SLC26A6' and 'offer the first partial view of the STAS domain previously predicted to be unstructured.' Reviewer 3 notes 'the structural data is also of high quality and is the first structure of an SLC26 coupled anion exchanger.' The editor describes this as providing 'the first partial view of the previously unresolved IVS region.'

results.result: SLC26A6 functions as a strictly coupled transporter that exchanges Cl⁻ with HCO₃⁻ at a 1:1 stoichiometric ratio in an electroneutral manner. This was demonstrated through multiple assays: no detectable currents in patch clamp electrophysiology, no acidification in ACMA assays, robust Cl⁻ transport in lucigenin assays without valinomycin requirement, and HCO₃⁻ influx detected by europium probe that is enhanced by Cl⁻ gradients.
results.evaluation: Reviewers unanimously support this characterization. Reviewer 1 states the data shows 'unequivocally that purified recombinant SLC26A6 reconstituted in proteoliposomes mediates electroneutral chloride/bicarbonate exchange.' Reviewer 2 notes the authors 'provide compelling evidence to support the idea that SLC26A6's exchange anions at equimolar stoichiometry, leading to the electroneutral...transport of HCO₃⁻/Cl⁻.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'the claims in this manuscript are all well-supported by the data' and praises the 'comprehensive functional analysis.'

results.result: SLC26A6 mediates coupled Cl⁻/oxalate exchange, which would be electrogenic due to the 1:1 exchange of monovalent Cl⁻ with divalent oxalate. This was demonstrated by robust ACMA fluorescence decrease upon oxalate addition to Cl⁻-loaded proteoliposomes, though electrogenic currents could not be detected by patch clamp electrophysiology, likely due to slow kinetics.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 identifies this as a weakness, noting 'the inconsistent, technique-dependent detection of SLC26A6-mediated electrogenic chloride/oxalate exchange. In particular whole cell currents attributable to SLC26A6 in SLC26A6-expressing HEK293 cells in an oxalate bath could not be detected, whereas robust, saturable Cl⁻ efflux into oxalate solution from proteoliposomes...was detectable by AMCA fluorescence decay.' The authors acknowledge the mechanism is 'not shown unambiguously' and is 'assumed' based on the functional data.

results.result: The SLC26A6 structure represents an inward-facing conformation that closely resembles SLC26A9, with TMs superimposing at 1.3 Å RMSD. Both structures show segregation into core and gate domains, with the substrate binding site in the core domain accessible from the cytoplasm via an aqueous cavity while the extracellular exit is sealed. The gate domains form a rigid scaffold with the STAS domains, while core domains represent mobile elements.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these structural comparisons without challenge. Reviewer 2 notes 'the structure of SLC26A6 reveals a close resemblance to the fast, uncoupled Cl⁻ transporter SLC26A9, with the major structural differences observed within the anion binding site.' Reviewer 3 states 'the structural analysis, including the assignment of the chloride binding site, is also convincing' and notes 'the structural details and the chloride binding site are well-conserved among SLC26s.'

results.result: The altered anion selectivity between SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 results from a remodeled ion binding site in the mobile core domain. Key differences include: (1) a ~12-14° rotation of helix α10 between the two paralogs, (2) substitutions that reduce side chain volume in SLC26A9 (Ser96→Gly77, Val100→Gly81, Val407→Ala396, Gln408→Val397, Thr411→Ala400), and (3) most prominently, replacement of Arg404 in SLC26A6 with Val393 in SLC26A9. This creates a deeper binding pocket in SLC26A9 with lower field strength, while SLC26A6 has a shallower pocket where Arg404 increases positive electrostatic potential and likely stabilizes HCO₃⁻ and oxalate.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly support these structural insights. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'define a residue in surrounding the anion binding pocket which explains part of the difference in anion exchange coupling between SLC26A6 and SLC26A9.' Reviewer 2 notes the authors 'show that the size and charge variance of the binding pocket between the two paralogs could, in part, contribute to the differences in their transport mechanisms.' Reviewer 3 adds 'the authors present an interesting discussion comparing the structures of SLC26A5, SLC26A6, and SLC26A9, and how the details of the chloride binding site might influence the mechanistic distinctions.'

results.result: The R404V mutation in SLC26A6 compromises coupled Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ exchange and instead facilitates slow uncoupled Cl⁻ transport. The mutant shows small currents in patch clamp (not significantly higher than WT), confirmed uncoupled Cl⁻ transport in ACMA assays, but no pronounced Cl⁻ flux in lucigenin assays for coupled exchange. However, the mutation is insufficient to confer the complete functional phenotype of SLC26A9 as a fast uncoupled Cl⁻ conductor.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly supports this finding, stating the authors 'define a single Arg residue of the SLC26A6 transmembrane domain required for coupled exchange, mutation of which yields apparently uncoupled electrogenic chloride transport mechanistically resembling that of SLC26A9, although of lower magnitude.' However, Reviewer 1 also notes as a weakness 'an incomplete explanation of the mechanistic determinants of anion exchange coupling in SLC26A6 vs. uncoupled anion transport by SLC26A9,' acknowledging the single mutation is insufficient for full conversion.

results.result: SLC26A9 and SLC26A6 are mechanistically distinguished by the sequence of conformations in their transport cycles. In uncoupled SLC26A9, the transporter transitions between inward- and outward-facing states at high rates underlying pronounced currents. In coupled SLC26A6, conformational changes in the unloaded state are kinetically unfavorable, as evidenced by lack of currents and absence of Cl⁻ leak. The basis for these distinctive kinetic features and the nature of the energy barrier preventing unloaded state shuttling in SLC26A6 remain unclear.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 identifies this as a weakness: 'One is an incomplete explanation of the mechanistic determinants of anion exchange coupling in SLC26A6 vs. uncoupled anion transport by SLC26A9.' The authors themselves acknowledge uncertainty, stating 'The basis for the distinctive kinetic features of both paralogs is currently still unclear' and 'The nature of the energy barrier...has thus far remained elusive.' The speculation about a possible 'leaky channel-like conformation in SLC26A9' is noted to lack structural evidence.

results.result: The IVS region (Cα^IVS) contacts the loop connecting α8 and α9 of the mobile core domain, presumably influencing conformational preferences and potentially impacting transport. In SLC26A6, additional contacts with the IVS stabilize the inward-facing conformation. Similar interactions in full-length SLC26A9 may account for increased activity when the IVS is removed, though C-terminal truncation might also contribute. The role of C-terminal extensions in cellular regulation remains unclear.
results.evaluation: These claims are largely speculative interpretations of structural observations. The authors use language like 'presumably influences,' 'appear to further stabilize,' 'might have contributed,' and 'hints at a possible regulation.' Reviewers do not explicitly validate or challenge these interpretations, and Reviewer 1 notes the structure provides 'the first partial view of the STAS domain previously predicted to be unstructured' but does not comment on the functional implications proposed by the authors.

results.result: The core domains of SLC26A6 show close structural resemblance to SLC26A5 (Prestin) with RMSD of 1.13 Å despite functional differences (Prestin is a motor protein rather than transporter). Both share similar ion binding properties for Cl⁻ and HCO₃⁻. Similar anion interactions are found in SLC26A4 (Pendrin). While Prestin undergoes some conformational changes, the full transition to an outward-facing conformation appears prohibited.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly supports this comparison: 'the authors present an interesting discussion comparing the structures of SLC26A5, SLC26A6, and SLC26A9, and how the details of the chloride binding site might influence the mechanistic distinctions between these similar transporters.' The structural comparisons are based on published structures and are not challenged by reviewers.

results.result: Murine SLC26A9 mediates large, selective Cl⁻ currents that reverse at the Nernst potential, distinguishing it as an uncoupled chloride transporter. The ohmic currents lack time-dependence and show a lyotropic permeability sequence (Cl⁻, isothiocyanate, I⁻, nitrate) but efficiently discriminate against HCO₃⁻ and sulfate.
results.evaluation: These are established findings from prior work that reviewers accept as context. Reviewer 1 notes 'Both functions contrast with the uncoupled chloride conductance mediated by SLC26A9' and Reviewer 3 states 'the functional comparison with SLC26A9, which permits fast, passive chloride transport, in order to benchmark the SLC26A6 activity' is a strength. The characterization is used as a benchmark for comparison.

results.result: Background claims about the SLC26 family, including their diversity (uncoupled transporters, coupled exchangers, motor proteins), conservation across kingdoms, structural features (homodimeric architecture, core and gate domains, elevator mechanism), and prior characterization of specific paralogs including SLC26A6's tissue expression, role in oxalate transport, interaction with CFTR, and controversial stoichiometry reports.
results.evaluation: These are background/context claims supported by citations to prior literature. Reviewers do not challenge these established facts. The editor notes the study 'provides broadly relevant insights into the mechanistic diversity of the SLC26 transporters' in the context of this known diversity. Reviewer 1 notes 'In the setting of past conflicting results, the current work also contributes to the weight of previous evidence' regarding electroneutral exchange.

results.result: Additional observations including that both SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 interact with Cl⁻ with similar mM affinity via distinct interactions, core and gate domains bury similar contact areas in inward-facing conformations, C-termini contain PDZ binding motifs, and the study provides novel insight into structural basis of substrate selectivity and mechanistic distinctions.
results.evaluation: These are supporting observations and summary statements that reviewers implicitly accept. The editor's assessment that this is an 'important manuscript' that 'provides broadly relevant insights' aligns with the authors' summary claim. Reviewers praise the comprehensive approach without challenging these specific observations.

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support the structural determination of SLC26A6 (C4, C57-C66). OpenEval emphasizes the 3.3 Å cryo-EM resolution and structural comparisons with SLC26A9. Peer reviewers unanimously praise the 'novel cryo-EM structure' and 'first partial view of the STAS domain.' However, OpenEval R1 covers additional claims (C70-C83) about detailed structural comparisons that peer R1 does not explicitly address.

Both address structural comparisons with SLC26A9 (C72-C79). OpenEval R1 includes these claims as part of broader structural characterization with RMSD values. Peer R4 accepts these structural comparisons, with Reviewer 2 noting 'close resemblance to...SLC26A9' and Reviewer 3 stating 'structural details...are well-conserved among SLC26s.'

Perfect agreement on electroneutral exchange characterization (C40-C50). Both evaluations strongly support the claims with converging evidence from multiple assays. OpenEval cites patch clamp, lucigenin-based Cl- flux, and europium probe data. Peer reviewers use terms like 'unequivocally' and 'compelling evidence' for the electroneutral Cl-/HCO3- exchange. Peer R2 additionally includes C5, C56, C112 as part of this evaluation.

Both address oxalate transport (C52-C55, C113, C116-C117) but with different confidence levels. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, finding the ACMA assay data robust and the inference of electrogenic transport 'logically sound.' Peer review rates as UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 1 identifying 'inconsistent, technique-dependent detection' as a weakness, particularly the failure to detect whole cell currents while observing ACMA fluorescence decay.

Strong agreement on structural basis for selectivity differences (C7, C90-C102, C120-C124). Both evaluations support the identification of Arg404 as a key residue and the structural analysis of pocket geometry. OpenEval emphasizes RMSD calculations and structural data. Peer reviewers note the authors 'define a residue...which explains part of the difference' and discuss how 'size and charge variance of the binding pocket' contributes to mechanistic differences.

Perfect claim overlap (C103-C111) with agreement on R404V mutation effects. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval describes it as 'well-designed structure-function experiment' showing uncoupled transport and loss of coupled exchange. Peer Reviewer 1 confirms the mutation 'yields apparently uncoupled electrogenic chloride transport' but notes as a weakness the 'incomplete explanation' since single mutation is insufficient for full conversion to SLC26A9-like function.

Both address mechanistic differences between paralogs (C129-C135) but with different confidence. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, stating the mechanistic model 'provides a coherent explanation' while acknowledging 'exact energy barriers remain to be fully elucidated.' Peer review rates as UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 1 identifying 'incomplete explanation of mechanistic determinants' as a weakness and authors acknowledging the basis 'is currently still unclear.'

Perfect claim overlap (C86-C89, C125-C128) on structural conservation within SLC26 family. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes RMSD comparison with Prestin and conserved arginine residue. Peer Reviewer 3 explicitly supports this, calling it 'an interesting discussion comparing the structures of SLC26A5, SLC26A6, and SLC26A9' and how binding site details 'might influence the mechanistic distinctions.'
